BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, particles, and VFX. Thirty-five terms for particle effects from what spawns and when, to how particles move and look, which engine parts do the work and how to design and effect. The exact term tells an agent precisely what to change.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often think amount is how many particles are born each second. It is not. Amount is how many one emission cycle holds so it caps how many are alive. The birth rate is amount divided by lifetime. This film goes through the terms each one shown so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Eight labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list, computed. The numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map. 35 terms about particle effects, short-lived points that look like fire, smoke, or a burst in four groups. The first group is what spawns and when. Particle, emitter, particle system, amount, lifetime, steady state, explosiveness, one shot, and pre-process.

B0102.heard: The second group is how it moves and looks. Emission shape, initial velocity, spread, seed, gravity, damping, scale curve, color ramp, texture, additive blending and billboard. These say where particles start, how they move and change, and how each one is drawn.

B0103.heard: The third group is engine parts and cost. Local Coords, fixed FPS, visibility rec, the GPU and CPU nodes which run on the graphics card or on the processor, the process material, sub-emitter, trail and particle shader, which node which rules and where the work lands.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is designing the effect, reads, restraint, shape language, color coding, analogous colors and timing curve. These say how a VFX artist, a visual effects artist, makes an effect clear and easy to tell apart.

B0201.heard: This drawing follows one dot through its life. A particle is one small, short-lived sprite or mesh inside an effect. It is born moves by the rules and dies when it reaches its lifetime. In this simulated run it is born on the left, reaches the top at 1.1 seconds and dies at 2.2. For example, when the player dies in the Walker Dodge game, each dot that flies out of the death burst is one particle.

B0202.heard: The dark square at the bottom is the emitter, the thing that spawns particles. It is the spawner, not the points it makes. Here it fires 12 a second and each dot rises, fades and dies so 19 are alive out of 36 born. For example, when a mob touches the player in the Walker Dodge game, code moves the bursts emitter to the spot where the player was so the new particles are born there.

B0203.heard: The red box lists the rules. A particle system is the emitter plus the rules for its particles, where they start, how fast they go, and how long each one lasts. Here the rules say speeds of 230 to 330, gravity 220, and a lifetime of 1.5 seconds. For example, a campfire in your level is one particle system, a spawn point at the log's plus rules that send embers up and fade them out.

B0301.heard: This chart will count the particles alive over six seconds. The setting amount is how many particles one emission cycle holds, and so the most a looping emitter can ever have alive. In this simulated chart, the red dashed line marks amount at 60, a ceiling the count cannot pass. Its look-alike emission rate is birth per second. For example, a looping torch in your level with amount 60 never shows more than 60 flames at once, however long it burns.

B0302.heard: The black bar under the axis is the lifetime two seconds here. The setting lifetime is how many seconds each particle lasts before it dies. It is also the length of one emission cycle, so here one cycle takes two seconds. For example, the death burst in the Walker Dodge game use is a short lifetime, so its dots are gone soon after the hit and the screen is clear again.

B0303.heard: Now tick marks along the bottom show each birth. Spread 60 births over a 2 second cycle and you get 30 born per second. That is the emission rate, amount divided by lifetime and it is not the same as amount. For example, if you give the dust behind a running player a longer lifetime and leave amount alone, fewer puffs are born each second and each one hangs around longer.

B0304.heard: The count of particles alive climbs for two seconds and then goes flat. Steady state means birth equal deaths, so the number alive levels off. After one lifetime, as many particles die each moment as are born and the count stays at 60. For example, the spray at the foot of a waterfall in your level fills in over its first moments, then holds its steady state for as long as the player stands and watches.

B0401.heard: In this simulated run, three rows of tick marks show when 32 particles are born in one cycle of 0.6 seconds. The setting explosiveness decides how bunched the berths are. At zero they spread across the whole cycle. At 0.5 they crowd into the first half, and at one they all come at the start. For example, the coin pick up burst and the Walker 3D platformer sets explosiveness to one. So every sparkle appears the instant the coin is taken.

B0402.heard: Now all 32 appear together in a ring and fly out and they will die together. That is a burst, which in Godo simply means explosiveness set to one. Here all 32 are still alive at 0.33 seconds. For example, the death burst in AI coding agent added to the Walker Dodge game uses explosiveness one, so every dot leaves the spot where the player was hit at the same instant.

B0403.heard: Two timelines over three seconds compare one shot with looping. The setting one shot means only one emission cycle happens and then the emitter stops. Without it, cycles repeat forever which is looping. Here the looping emitter gives 160 births in three seconds and the one shot emitter only 32. For example, in the Walker 3D platformer an enemy's explosion is one shot, while the globe behind each bullet keeps looping.

B0404.heard: The gray line climbs from empty while the red line starts full. The setting pre-process also called pre-warm starts and effect as if it had already been running for that many seconds. Without pre-process the first frame has one particle alive. With pre-process of two seconds the full lifetime here it has 60. For example chimney smoke in a level should already be rising when the level loads. So you set pre-process instead of letting the player watch it start from nothing.

B0501.heard: Three boxes each with 40 spawn points from a seated simulation. The mission shape is the volume particles are born in. A point puts them all on one spot, a sphere scatters them through a ball, and a box spreads them through a block. Its neighbor spread is about direction, not where they start. For example, the coin burst in the Walker 3D platformer uses a sphere emission shape, so its sparkles start all around the coin, not from a single spot.

B0502.heard: Arrows fan up from one point each as long as it's speed. Initial velocity is the speed and direction a particle starts with. Each particle takes its speed from a range, here 150 to 300 pixels per second, and in this seated run the speed's drawn land between 150 and 285. For example, the dust kicked up when the player lands from a jump wants a slow initial velocity. So the puffs drift out instead of shooting away.

B0503.heard: Three fans of 24 rays all aimed up. The setting spread is the cone angle of random variation around the emission direction. A spread of zero is a single beam, 45 is a fan, and 180 goes every way, so only 54% of those rays still point upward. In 3D, every way includes toward the screen. For example, the death burst in the Walker Dodge game uses a spread of 180. So its dots fly out in every direction.

B0504.heard: Three boxes show 10 particles after 0.6 seconds. A seed is the starting number for the random choices, and determinism means the same seed and inputs give the same output every run. Seed 7 run twice matches to 0.0 pixels. Seed 8 lands up to 117.1 pixels away. For example, a test run from the command line can fix the seed of a spark effect, then check that two runs match exactly.

B0601.heard: 12 particles fly for 1.2 seconds. Gravity for particles is a constant downward acceleration. Each step adds a little downward speed, so a straight path, the gray dashes, bends into an arc, the red lines. With gravity 300, the mean drop in this simulated run is 219 pixels, near the formula's 216. For example, sparks from a smashed crate in a platformer arc up and fall back to the floor because their effect has gravity.

B0602.heard: Two rows of dots won every tenth of a second starting at 300. Damping is the rate at which particles lose speed. A damping of 100 takes a speed of 100 to 0 in one second. With no damping, the dots keep going. With damping 150, they stop after two seconds. 299 pixels out. For example, smoke from a car's exhaust pipe in your game shoots out and then hangs in the air because of damping.

B0603.heard: A curve sits above a row of dots that shrink with age. A scale curve sets a particle's size over its life. It takes the particle's age from zero at birth to one at death and gives back a size. At age 0.6 the size is about 64% of full, and at age 1 it is zero. For example, the trail behind the player in the Walker Dodge game uses a scale curve, so each faded copy of the player shrinks.

B0604.heard: A gradient bar runs from orange at age 0 to almost nothing at age 1. A color ramp is a gradient for particle color over its life. It does for color what the scale curve does for size. The red numbers under the circles are alpha, the opacity, falling from 1 to 0. So at age 0.5 the alpha is 0.5. For example, the death burst in the Walker Dodge game fades from solid white to transparent through a color ramp.

B0701.heard: The same burst of 32 particles drawn twice. The texture is the image drawn for each particle. If it is null, not set. Each particle is one pixel square. On the left, null covers 32 pixels, 0.009% of the screen. On the right, a 16 by 16 radial dot covers about 6,434. For example, the first death burst an agent built for the Walker Dodge game had no texture. So it was 32 single pixels.

B0702.heard: Two dark squares each with three overlapping glows. Addive blending is a blend mode that adds the new color to what is behind it. Where glows overlap, the light piles up and gets brighter up to the limit of 255. It's look-alike alpha blending mixes by opacity and stays dull. The right hand center is much brighter. For example, the particle material file in the Walker 3D platformer uses additive blending, so it's glows bright and where they overlap. Well, let's...

B0703.heard: Two rows of squares as the camera turns around the effect. A billboard is a flat quad, a square card that always turns to face the camera. It is also called a camera facing card. The dark flat quad does not turn, so at 80 degrees it is only 17 pixels wide. The red billboard stays 100 pixels wide and never goes edge on. For example, the particle material in the Walker 3D platformer turns on billboarding. So every glow faces the player's camera.

B0801.heard: Two lanes each with an emitter moving to the right. The setting local chords decides whose coordinates the particles use. Off the default means world coordinates. Each particle stays where it was born so the top lane leaves dots behind. On means local coordinates. Particles ride with the emitter so the bottom lane carries its cloud along. For example, sparkles circling a player who has picked up a shield should use local chords so they stay wrapped around the player as the player runs.

B0802.heard: One particle's height over a second. Fixed FPS updates particles at a fixed rate, not every frame, and interpolate smooths the motion between those updates. Here the rate is slowed on purpose to five times a second. The dark steps miss the true gray curve by up to 128 pixels, the red interpolated line by only eight. For example, a smoke effect in the background can update less often to save work. Within interpolate on so it still moves smoothly.

B0803.heard: Two camera views move right. The visibility wrecked is the region that must be on screen for the effect to run. In this made up example, the top wrecked 30 pixels each way has left the view, so the effect stops with its particles still on screen. The lower wrecked 130 pixels each way still overlaps, so it runs. For example, a bonfire scrolling levels edge vanishes early if its visibility wrecked is smaller than its flames.

B0901.heard: A table asks which of five properties each node type has from the engine's own class list. GPU Particles 2D and its 3D twin are simulated on the GPU, the graphics card. They handle many particles and have more features. They run a material of rules and only they have sub emitters, trails and particle shaders. The GPU node has four of these five, for example. The Death Burst in the Walker Dodge game is a GPU Particles 2D node, a child of the main scene.

B0902.heard: The CPU column fills in. CPU particles 2D and its 3D twin are simulated on the CPU, the processor. They run on a wider range of hardware but handle fewer particles. The CPU node has only one of the five emission shape. Its cost rises with every particle. Measured on one machine, 1000 costs 0.035 milliseconds of frame, and 50,000 costs 1.61. For example, the coin burst in the Walker 3D platformer uses the 3D CPU node.

B0903.heard: Three boxes split an effect into a mission, process and draw. Particle process material is the resource that holds a GPU particle systems rules for moving and changing. Amount, lifetime, explosiveness and one shot sit on the node. Velocity, spread, gravity, scale curve and color ramp sit in this material. Texture, blend mode and billboard belong to drawing. For example, the death burst in the Walker Dodge game keeps it spread. Its speed range and its color ramp in a particle process material.

B1001.heard: Six sparks have died, each leaving a cluster of puffs. A sub-emitter is a second GPU particle system that spawns particles from the first one's particles. In this simulated run, each of six sparks leaves five puffs when it dies, so no sparks remain and 30 puffs are alive. It's look-alike the trail follows one moving object instead. For example, fireworks sparks that each pop into a tiny cloud of smoke as they die use a sub-emitter. It's only a GPU node offers.

B1002.heard: A red ribbon curves behind a dark moving head. A trail or ribbon is a strip that follows a moving object textured to look like a tail. It joins the head's last 30 positions and thins and fades toward the end. Here it is 446 pixels long. For example, a ribbon behind a thrown magic dagger shows the arkett flu. The node named trail in the Walker Dodge game is not a ribbon. It stamps faded copies of the player.

B1003.heard: Code in the dark box moves these dots. A particle shader sets each particle's properties in two functions. The start function runs once for each new particle, here setting its velocity. The process function runs on every step, here adding gravity times the time step. At step 22, the vertical velocity is 95.6 and the dot is 16 pixels up. For example, when the process materials checkboxes cannot describe a swirling spell. You swap that material for a particle shader.

B1101.heard: A fireball built in layers starts with a glowing head. Primary to tertiary read is the order the eye notices and affects parts, the head first, then the tail, then the sparks. The primary read is what the eye finds first, here a bright glow texture on a camera facing card. In this made up example it holds all of the visual weight so far. For example, in a spell that fires a bolt at an enemy, the bright core of the bolt is the primary read.

B1102.heard: A tail now streams off the head. The secondary read is that tail, a ribbon with a texture scrolling along it to suggest motion. The eye finds it after the head. In this made up example, the head keeps 57% of the visual weight and the tail takes 43. For example, the streak behind a fireball thrown in your game is its secondary read. It tells the player which way the ball is flying once the eye has found the glow.

B1103.heard: A few small sparks scatter around the tail. The tertiary read is small support that the eye finds last. It adds life, but too many sparks would pull weight away from the head. Here the sparks hold just 1% of the visual weight. The primary read is found first, and the tertiary read last. For example, a handful of embers drifting off a torch flame in a dungeon level are a tertiary read.

B1104.heard: Two bar charts show how loud each effect is in made up numbers. Restraint means keeping most effects modest so the important ones stand out. On the left, all five are loud and none stands out. On the right, one is loud and four are quiet, so the top effect is 3.3 times the others against 1.0. For example, if every coin footstep and jump flashes brightly, the death burst gets lost, so you tone the small effects down.

B1201.heard: Three icons in the same blue, each with a different meaning. Shape language means using the same shapes for the same meaning across the whole game. A plus with four arms means heal. A ring with no corners means shield, and a star with eight spikes means damage. Even in a crowded fight, the shape tells them apart. For example, if every healing pickup and healing spell in your game shows a plus, players learn that a plus means health.

B1202.heard: Four colored circles each with its hue angle on the color wheel. Color coding means using colors to signal team, damage type, or tone. Red marks team A at 0 degrees, green marks team B at 138, oranges fire at 30, and blue is ice at 195. Red and green are easy to tell apart at glance. For example, if every ice attack in your game glows light blue, players know a blue hit means ice damage.

B1203.heard: Three pairs of colors, a caster color around an effect color. Analogous colors are neighboring hues on the color wheel, used to tie an effect to the model that casts it. 20 degrees apart and 15 degrees apart both look related. 175 degrees apart clashes. Here neighboring means within 30 degrees. For example, a purple wizard in your game should cast a violet spell, not a yellow one, so players see it once who cast it.

B1204.heard: Explosion radius over time grown two ways. A timing curve varies how fast an effect grows and slows instead of using a constant rate. The gray line grows at a steady rate. The red one starts fast and then slows. At 40% of the time, the steady one has reached 40% of its size in the eased 178. For example, a grenade blast in your game that bursts out quickly and then settles feels powerful while a steady growth feels flat.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets two look alike terms side by side. On the left amount how many a cycle holds stays at 60 whether the lifetime is 2 seconds or 4. On the right emission rate born per second falls from 30 a second to 15. Twice the life half the rate.

B1302.heard: Local coordinates on the left carry the particles along with the emitter. World coordinates on the right leave each particle where it was born, so the dots are left behind as the emitter moves away.

B1303.heard: The setting one shot runs one emission cycle and then stops, so it gives 32 births in three seconds. Looping repeats the cycle forever, so it gives 160 births in the same three seconds.

B1304.heard: Gravity adds speed downward on every step, so the path bends down into an arc. Damping takes speed away on every step, so the dots bunch up and slow to a stop. One bends the path, the other shortens it.

B1401.heard: Each row turns a vague request into an exact instruction. The smoke should already be rising, becomes set pre-processed to two seconds, the lifetime, so the first frame is already full. On frame one, one particle is alive without it, and sixty with it.

B1402.heard: I want a burst, not a stream becomes set explosiveness to 1 and 1 shot to true, with amount 32. With explosiveness 0, the burst spread out evenly, a few in each tenth of a second. With explosiveness 1, all 32 come in the first tenth of a second.

B1403.heard: The burst looks like specks of dust becomes, give it a 16 by 16 radial texture because null means single pixel squares. Null covers 32 pixels and the dot covers 6434 about 200 times the area.

B1404.heard: The 2D burst looks thin becomes, turn on particle flag disable Z, so no speed goes into the Z-axis that a 2D camera never shows. Over 2,000 seated directions, only 78% of the speed shows without it, and all of it with it.

B1405.heard: The test never sees finished becomes set the flag through a dictionary because a lambda cannot reassign a local variable. The signal fired both times but a true or false flag set inside the lambda still showed false and the dictionary showed true.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a particle effect. First, is the effect's parents still visible when it fires. A burst under a hidden player can be emitting and still unseen. A headless test proves state. Only a screen shows the effect.

B1502.heard: Second is the texture set and is disable Z on in 2D. Without a texture, each particle is a tiny dot and without disable Z part of its speed goes into an axis the camera cannot see.

B1503.heard: Third, do amount lifetime and explosiveness give the count and timing you meant. Work out the rate, amount divided by lifetime, and check whether the births spread out or come all at once.

B1504.heard: Fourth does a one-shot effect restart on every later use. A burst that fires on the first death and never again passes a quick test and fails in the second game.

B1505.heard: Fifth is the visibility wrecked big enough and is overdraw cheap on a real GPU. A headless run measures neither because nothing is drawn. Large, overlapping, transparent particles cost drawing time on real hardware.

B1506.heard: 6. Did a person watch it on a screen and does it read as one clear effect? A headless test proves state. Only a person or screen can say whether the effect looks like anything.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, a particle is one short-lived point and the emitter is what spawns it. Amount caps how many are alive and the rate is amount divided by lifetime. Explosiveness 1 makes a burst and 1 shot stops after a single cycle. Gravity adds speed downward and damping takes speed away. A GPU node keeps its movement rules and its particle process material. Restraint keeps most effects quiet so the important one reads clearly.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on particle effect terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use the terms amount, emission rate, lifetime, explosiveness, one-shot, pre-process, spread, initial velocity, gravity, and damping. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms, particles and VFX at Nick Bear Brown.
